1 About metastatic NSCLC
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is
the most common type of lung cancer.
Treatment for widespread NSCLC
combined with supportive care improves
lives. This guide explains how the growth
of widespread cancer can be slowed and
how symptoms can be eased.
What is metastatic NSCLC?
Metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
is an abnormal spreading of certain types of
lung cancer cells into the lining of the lung or
to another organ.
This description is important because
treatment differs between lung cancer types
and where lung cancer is in the body.
Types of NSCLC
NSCLC is a group of cancer

atment differs between lung cancer types
and where lung cancer is in the body.
Types of NSCLC
NSCLC is a group of cancers. Each cancer in
this group affects a different type of lung cell.
You have NSCLC if you have one of the
following lung cancers:
 Adenocarcinoma (A-deh-noh-KAR-sih-
NOH-muh) affects cells in the airways that
make mucus.
 Large cell carcinoma (kar-sin-OH-ma)
forms from large cells in the airways.
 Squamous (SQUAY-mous) cell carcinoma
affects cells that form on airways in
response to toxic exposure.
There are more types of NSCLC, but they are
much less common. Some lung cancers are a
mix of cell types.
Metastatic sites of NSCLC
Lung cancer is a disease that causes lung
ce

ommon. Some lung cancers are a
mix of cell types.
Metastatic sites of NSCLC
Lung cancer is a disease that causes lung
cells to grow out of control and form a tumor
on the wall of the airway.
Airways of the lungs
The airways are tube-shaped
passages that branch out
like a tree in your lungs.
Non-small cell lung cancer
causes cells from the inner
wall of the airways to grow
out of control.

1 About metastatic NSCLC
Lung cancer cells can also break away from
a lung tumor, spread outside of the lung, and
form more tumors. Cancer that has spread
from where it started is called metastatic.
NSCLC can spread to many different places.
It often spreads to the brain, liver, bone, and
adrenal glands. NSCLC also spreads into the
tissue lining around the lung and from one lung
to the other.
How is metastatic NSCLC
treated?
Treatment of metastatic NSCLC is based on
features of the cancer, your overall health, and
your goals for treatment. There’s no single
treatment plan that’s best for everyone.
Testing is needed

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.8 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
rall health, and
your goals for treatment. There’s no single
treatment plan that’s best for everyone.
Testing is needed to plan treatment
Your care team will need to know the type of
lung cancer and where the cancer is. They will
also test for important cancer features called
biomarkers. To see a list of tests needed to
plan treatment, read Chapter 2: Testing for
metastatic NSCLC.
Supportive care addresses the
challenges of cancer
Supportive care involves multiple types of
aid that improve quality of life. Receiving
supportive care early has been shown to
extend and enhance life for people with lung
cancer. Read more about this important part
of cancer care in Chapter 3: Improving life with

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.8 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
life for people with lung
cancer. Read more about this important part
of cancer care in Chapter 3: Improving life with
supportive care.
Confused about
lung cancer?
People use the term lung cancer to
describe many cancers. Sometimes, they
misuse the term, so here’s an explanation
of what lung cancer is and what it isn’t.
What lung cancer is
Simply, lung cancer is a disease that
causes uncontrolled growth of lung cells.
There are many types of lung cells, so
there are many types of lung cancer.
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is
the most common type of lung cancer.
So when people talk about lung cancer,
they’re likely talking about NSCLC.
What lung cancer isn't
Cancers that have spread to

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.8 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
n people talk about lung cancer,
they’re likely talking about NSCLC.
What lung cancer isn't
Cancers that have spread to the lungs are
not lung cancers. For example, stomach
cancer that has spread to the lungs is still
stomach cancer.
In addition to this guide, the library of
NCCN Guidelines for Patients has guides
for metastatic NSCLC, other types of lung
cancer, and cancers that have spread
to the lungs. The library can be found at
NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the
NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

1 About metastatic NSCLC
Systemic therapy is the most
common treatment
Systemic therapy consists of prescribed drugs
that treat cancer throughout the entire body.
It’s the focus of this guide because it’s used
to treat most metastatic lung cancers.
Less often, local treatment is used to try to
cure limited metastases. For example, surgery
or radiation therapy may be done to control
lung cancer that has spread only to an adrenal
gland.
People with metastatic lung cancer are
often on systemic therapy for the rest of
their lives. Typically, a person takes one
treatment then switches to another if the
cancer grows again

for the rest of
their lives. Typically, a person takes one
treatment then switches to another if the
cancer grows again. The types and order of
systemic therapy are discussed in Chapters 4
through 6. Each chapter focuses on a specific
biomarker type of NSCLC.
Clinical trials offer hope
Clinical trials are a type of health research
that aim to find better ways of treating cancer.
Often, standard treatment is compared to a
promising new drug. A clinical trial may be an
option for you. Learn more about clinical trials
in Chapter 6: Treatment by NSCLC type.

more satisfied when they actively take part
in planning their cancer care.
The NCCN Guidelines for Patients will help
you play a larger role in your care. Discuss the
recommendations in this guide with your care
team. Ask questions about your options and
share your goals and concerns.
Don’t know what to ask? You’re not alone.
That’s why we include suggested questions to
ask at the end of chapters.
Keep reading to find the best care for you.

2 Testing for metastatic NSCLC
Several tests are needed to confirm lung
cancer and plan treatment. Your care
team will test for the type of lung cancer,
extent of the cancer, and for cancer
markers. They will also collect information
on your overall health.
Many times, metastatic non-small cell lung
cancer (NSCLC) is suspected because of
concerning symptoms. Less often, a mass that
may be cancer is found by accident on a scan
for another health issue. In this chapter, you’ll
learn how your care team:
 Decides where and how to remove tissue
samples for cancer testing
 Assesses the extent, or stage, of the
cancer in

m:
 Decides where and how to remove tissue
samples for cancer testing
 Assesses the extent, or stage, of the
cancer in your body
 Learns the type and features of the
cancer
 Evaluates your overall health
It takes a team
Lung cancer is confirmed, or diagnosed, by
testing samples of body tissue or fluid for
cancer cells. How tissue is removed for testing
differs between people. It partly depends on
where the cancer might be in your body.
A team of experts will decide the best way
to confirm if you have lung cancer. Your
diagnostic team may include these experts:
 A pulmonologist is an expert in lung
diseases.
 A thoracic radiologist is an expert in
reading pictures (images) of the inside

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.11 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
nologist is an expert in lung
diseases.
 A thoracic radiologist is an expert in
reading pictures (images) of the inside
of the chest.
 A thoracic surgeon is an expert in
performing operations within the chest.
 An interventional radiologist is an expert
in performing image-guided biopsies.
 A pathologist is an expert in tissue and
cells and confirming cancer.
You are an important part of the team. Your
input is just as important as tests for planning
treatment.
Lung cancer stages
and metastatic cancer
There are 4 main stages of lung cancer.
You may see them written with Roman
numerals—stages I (1), II (2), III (3), and
IV (4). Higher stages mean a greater
extent of cancer.
Stage 4 is met

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.11 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
Roman
numerals—stages I (1), II (2), III (3), and
IV (4). Higher stages mean a greater
extent of cancer.
Stage 4 is metastatic cancer at
diagnosis. The cancer has spread to
the lining of the lung or to other organs.
Sometimes, earlier stages of lung cancer
become metastatic after treatment.

2 Testing for metastatic NSCLC
Detecting cancer on imaging
Imaging shows the inside of the body and can
show where the cancer may be. Your team
will use imaging to decide the best place to
remove tissue samples for cancer testing.
Your team will also use imaging for cancer
staging. A cancer stage describes the extent
of lung cancer in the body. For many people,
diagnosis and cancer staging are done at
the same time. You will likely have 3 types
of imaging.
CT scan
Computed tomography (CT) is often the first
scan done to stage lung cancer. Your team will
look for tumors in images of your chest and
upper abdomen, inc

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.12 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
the first
scan done to stage lung cancer. Your team will
look for tumors in images of your chest and
upper abdomen, including the adrenal glands.
A CT scan is a more detailed kind of x-ray. It
takes many pictures from different angles. A
computer combines the images to make 3D
pictures.
You'll receive an injection of contrast if it's safe
for you. Contrast is a substance that makes
images clearer.
FDG-PET/CT scan
Positron emission tomography (PET)
combined with a CT scan is necessary if it has
not been done before. PET highlights tissue in
your body that may be cancerous. A PET/CT
scan may detect cancer that was not found by
CT alone or may show signs that the cancer
has spread.
Your whole

scan may detect cancer that was not found by
CT alone or may show signs that the cancer
has spread.
Your whole body may be scanned, or the scan
may extend from your neck to the middle of
your thighs.
Before the scan, you will be injected with a
tracer called fluorodeoxyglucose, or FDG.
The tracer makes cancer cells show up as
bright (or hot) spots on the scan. Multiple
health problems can cause hot spots, so hot
spots that suggest cancer often need to be
confirmed by other tests.

pictures of the inside of
your body. During the scan,

2 Testing for metastatic NSCLC
Brain MRI
Lung cancer tends to spread to the brain, so
it's very important to test if it has. Magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) may show small
brain tumors that aren’t causing symptoms.
MRI uses a safe magnetic field and radio
waves to make pictures. You’ll have a scan
with contrast and another scan without
contrast unless contrast is not safe for you.
If you can’t have an MRI, you may get a CT
scan of your head with contrast.
Confirming cancer with biopsy
A biopsy is a procedure that removes samples
of body tissue or fluid for cancer testing. Often,
tissue from the organ with the meta

a procedure that removes samples
of body tissue or fluid for cancer testing. Often,
tissue from the organ with the metastasis is
taken rather than from the lungs. Your team
will use imaging to select the biopsy site, which
is often the adrenal gland, liver, or bone.
Types of biopsy
The type of biopsy that will be done depends
on the body part and the experience of your
team. Common types of biopsies for metastatic
lung cancer are:
 An external needle biopsy involves
guiding a thin needle through your skin
and into a tumor. These biopsies include
transthoracic needle aspiration, core
needle biopsies, pericardiocentesis, and
thoracentesis.
 Down-the-throat biopsies is when
a thin tube is gu

needle biopsies, pericardiocentesis, and
thoracentesis.
 Down-the-throat biopsies is when
a thin tube is guided down your throat
into your airway (bronchus) or food pipe
(esophagus). These procedures include
many types of bronchoscopy.
 Keyhole surgeries involve making
small openings in your chest. Small tools
are inserted through the holes to remove
tissue. This method is less invasive
than open surgery. These surgeries
include laparoscopy and thoracoscopy.
Thoracoscopy is also called video-
assisted thoracoscopic surgery.

If NSCLC is found, the pathologist will identify
the type.
 Adenocarcinoma is a cancer of cells that
often line the air sacs in the lungs and
make mucus. This is the most common
type of NSCLC.
 Large cell carcinoma is a cancer of cells
that are larger than other cells in the
airways.
 Squamous cell carcinoma is a cancer
of thin, flat cells and often occurs in the
central part of a lung.
 There are also rare and mixed types of
NSCLC.
The results of lab tests used for diagnosis are
recorded in a pathology report.

After metastatic NSCLC is confirmed, your
care team

for diagnosis are
recorded in a pathology report.
Planning treatment
After metastatic NSCLC is confirmed, your
care team will focus on treating the cancer.
One member of your team will be a medical
oncologist. A medical oncologist is trained in
treating cancer with prescribed drugs.
A radiation oncologist may also be part of your
team. This specialist treats cancer or relieves
symptoms with radiation. Learn more about
symptom relief and other team members in
Chapter 3: Improving life with supportive care.
To plan treatment, your team will need to learn
more about the cancer and your overall health.
They will use your diagnostic test results and
the tests described next in this chapter. A
com

and your overall health.
They will use your diagnostic test results and
the tests described next in this chapter. A
complete list of tests for metastatic NSCLC
is in Guide 1.
You might need to get new scans. Scans done
more than 60 days ago should not be used to
decide your treatment.
Biopsy of metastasis
If your care team suspects
metastatic lung cancer, you may
have a biopsy of the metastasis
instead of the tumor in the lung.
A biopsy of the metastasis can
diagnose and stage the cancer at
the same time. A needle biopsy
through the skin may reach some
metastases, such as in the liver
(shown). Imaging is often used
to help guide the needle to the
correct spot.

Assessing your overall health
Your team will perform a thorough evaluation
of your health. They need to know about all
of your health issues, both those caused by
the cancer and those unrelated to the cancer.
They also need to determine all of the places
where the lung cancer has likely spread.
Medical history
Expect your team to ask a lot of questions
about your health. This is known as taking a
medical history. Your team will want to know
about your past and current health, such as:
 Illnesses and injuries
 Symptoms like unexplained weight loss,
trouble breathing, chest pain, and

[전이성 폐암 환자 안내 | p.15 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
t health, such as:
 Illnesses and injuries
 Symptoms like unexplained weight loss,
trouble breathing, chest pain, and cough
 Prescribed and over-the-counter
medicines and supplements
 Previous surgeries
 Lifestyle choices, including your diet, how
active you are, and whether you smoke or
drink alcohol
Also be prepared to discuss the health of
your close blood (first-degree) relatives. First-
degree relatives include siblings, parents, and
grandparents related to you by birth.
Physical exam
A team member will also perform a thorough
physical exam of your body.

Driver mutations help many lung cancers

What are driver mutations?
A driver mutation is an abnormal change in
the DNA of a cell that supports cancer growth.
It enables cancer cells to quickly duplicate,
survive, and spread in the body.
At this time, several driver mutations in non-
small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) have been
found. And researchers are looking for more.
Recommendations for driver mutation testing

Chemotherapy destroys any fast-growing cells
even if they’re not cancer cells. It was once the
only treatment for metastatic lung cancer.

driver mutations and harm fewer normal cells.
These newer treatments are called targeted
therapy.

cancer cells grow. Targeted therapy is a drug
treatment that stops these proteins.

The immune system is the body’s natural
defense against disease, including cancer. A
type of white blood cell called T cells are a key
part of this system. T cells that kill cancer cells
are called cytotoxic, or killer, T cells.
PD-1 limits T-cell activity
The immune system has brakes that control

immune response doesn’t damage the body.
PD-1 is a brake on T cells.

In some people with NSCLC, the immune
brakes are overused. The PD-1 brake is
activated when PD-L1 on cancer cells
attaches to it.

treatment days, followed by rest days.

6 Treatment by NSCLC type
Lung cancer differs among people by the
type of affected lung cell. Your treatment
will be specific to the type of lung
cancer you have. In addition to standard
treatment, a clinical trial may be an option
for you.
When lung cancer doesn’t have a driver
mutation or abnormal PD-L1 levels, treatment
is mainly based on the type of non-small cell
lung cancer (NSCLC). This chapter lists the
options for treatment.
Some options in this chapter are also
sometimes used to treat NSCLC with driver
mutations or abnormal PD-L1 levels as
explained in Chapters 4 and 5.

Planning treatment
Your care team will decide what treatments are
options for you.
The cancer treatments listed in this chapter
may not be safe if your performance status is
poor (either 3 or 4 on the Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group scoring system). These
scores suggest that cancer treatment would

Types of therapy
Most therapies for NSCLC consist of
chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or a
combination of both.
Chemotherapy
The classic treatment for widespread
metastatic lung cancer is chemotherapy. It kills
fast-growing cells, including cancer cells. One
or more chemotherapy drugs may be a part of
treatment.
Platinum-doublet chemotherapy consists of the
following 2 types of chemotherapy:
 The platinum-based chemotherapy is
either cisplatin or carboplatin.
 The second chemotherapy is pemetrexed
(Axtle, Alimta, Pemfexy, Pemrydi RTU),
paclitaxel, paclitaxel

gemcitabine (Avgemsi).
Platinum-doublet chemotherapy can cause
serious side effects, so you must be healthy
enough to get this treatment.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors
Immune checkpoint inhibitors restore the
ability of immune cells to kill cancer cells. They
treat lung cancer with PD-L1 as explained in
Chapter 5. But they may also extend life when
lung cancer does not have PD-L1.

Another way to obtain treatment is through a
clinical trial.
A clinical trial is a type of medical research
study. After being developed and tested in a
lab, potential new ways of fighting cancer need
to be studied in people.
If found to be safe and effective in a clinical
trial, a drug, device, or treatment approach
may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Who can enroll?
It depends on the clinical trial’s rules, called
eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age,
cancer type and stage, treatment history, or
general health. They ensure that participants
are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as
safe as possible for the participants.
Informed consent
Clinical trials are managed by a research
team. This group of experts will review the
study with you in detail, including its purpose
and the risks and benefits of joining. All of this
information is also provided in an informed
consent form. Read the form carefully and
ask questio

information is also provided in an informed
consent form. Read the form carefully and
ask questions before signing it. Take time to
discuss it with people you trust. Keep in mind
that you can leave and seek treatment outside
of the clinical trial at any time.
Will I get a placebo?
Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines)
are almost never used alone in cancer clinical
trials. It’s common to receive either a placebo
with a standard treatment, or a new drug with
a standard treatment. You will be informed,
verbally and in writing, if a placebo is part of a
clinical trial before you enroll.

including the study drug. But you may need

childcare, due to extra appointments. During
the trial, you will continue to receive standard
cancer care. This care is often covered by
insurance.

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is
the most common type of lung cancer.
Early and locally advanced cancers
haven't spread far from the lung. This
guide explains the treatments that may
cure or control the growth of these
cancers.
What are early and locally
advanced NSCLCs?
Early and locally advanced non-small cell lung

cells that have grown from the airways into
other lung tissue but haven't spread to other
organs.

There are more types of NSCLC, but they are
much less common. Some lung cancers are a
mix of cell types.
Growth of early and locally
advanced cancers
Lung cancer is a disease that causes lung
cells to grow out of control and form a tumor
on the wall of the airway.
Early and locally advanced lung cancers have
grown through the wall of the airway and into
other lung tissue. Some of these cancers have
also grown into or through the wall of the lung
and into other body tissue.
Some locally advanced NSCLCs have spread
to small structures, called lymph nodes, inside
of the

Some locally advanced NSCLCs have spread
to small structures, called lymph nodes, inside
of the lung or within the chest. But early and
locally advanced cancers have not spread to
the fluid within the lining around the lung or to
other organs.
Confused about
lung cancer?
People use the term lung cancer to
describe many cancers. Sometimes, they
misuse the term, so here’s an explanation
of what lung cancer is and what it isn’t.
What lung cancer is
Simply, lung cancer is a disease that
causes uncontrolled growth of lung cells.
There are many types of lung cells, so
there are many types of lung cancer.
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is
the most common type of lung can

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is

So when people talk about lung cancer,

What lung cancer isn't
Cancers that have spread to the lungs are
not lung cancers. For example, stomach

Tobacco smoke
The biggest risk factor for lung cancer is
smoking tobacco. The risk grows with the
number of cigarette packs you’ve smoked a
day and the years you’ve smoked. The risk
decreases with the number of years since
you’ve quit smoking.
Even if you don't smoke, exposure to second-
hand smoke increases the risk for lung cancer.
Second-hand smoke is smoke that has been
breathed out by a person smoking tobacco. It’s
also smoke from the burning tip of cigarettes,
cigars, or pipes.
Cancer-causing agents
You're more likely to get lung cancer after
exposure to:
 Radon
 Arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium,
nickel, and uranium
 Asbestos
 Coal smoke, soot, silica, and diesel fumes

Age
As you age, you are more likely to get lung
cancer. In recent years, half of the people
diagnosed with lung cancer were over 71
years of age. Only 6 out of 100 people with
lung cancer were under the age of 55 years at
the time of diagnosis.
Who gets lung cancer?
Experts are still learning why one person
gets lung cancer and another does not.
We know some of the risk factors that
increase a person’s chance for getting
lung cancer.
Yet people with many risk factors may
never get lung cancer, and people with
no risk factors sometimes get lung
cancer.

The risk for lung cancer increases after having

Hot spots
If you had a PET (positron emission
tomography) scan, the radiologist will look for
hot (or bright) spots.
Before the scan, a tracer was injected into
one of your veins. Cancer cells take in more of
injected tracer than normal cells and appear as
hot spots on the images.
Cancer is not the only health condition to
produce hots spots, so the cause often needs
to be confirmed by other testing.

What is lung cancer?
The lungs are the main organs of the
respiratory system. They deliver oxygen to
the blood and remove carbon dioxide from the
blood. The transfer of these gases in and out
of the body is called respiration.
Lung cancers form from cells that line the
airways of the lungs. The lungs' airways are
called the bronchus, bronchioli, and alveoli.

Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells.
They break the rules of cell growth.

becomes a mass of tissue called a tumor.
 Cancer cells grow out of control. They can

wall and invade other body parts.
 Cancer cells can break away from a
tumor and spread. They can enter the
bloodstream or a fluid called lymph and

1 Lung cancer basics » What are the symptoms of SCLC?
What are the symptoms of
SCLC?
SCLC can cause many types of symptoms.
The symptoms depend on where the lung
tumor has grown to or spread. SCLC can
prevent the lungs from getting the air they
need. Some people also have symptoms from
paraneoplastic syndromes, which are caused
by an abnormal body response to lung cancer.
Some symptoms caused by SCLC are listed in
Guide 1.
SCLC is often found when it’s causing
symptoms or routine blood tests are abnormal.
Less often, it’s found in x-rays or CT scans
before symptoms start. Unlike other lung
cancers, it’s difficult to detect SCLC ear

[소세포폐암 환자 가이드라인 | p.9 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
en, it’s found in x-rays or CT scans
before symptoms start. Unlike other lung
cancers, it’s difficult to detect SCLC early
because it grows more quickly.
Airways of the lungs
Air moves through your body in a series of airways. It travels down your throat and
through the windpipe (trachea). The windpipe splits into 2 airways called bronchi.
Inside the lung, each bronchus branches off into the parts of the lung, called lobes.
The right lung has 3 lobes, and the left lung has 2 lobes. The bronchi divide into
smaller airways called the bronchioli. At the end of the bronchioli are sacs called
alveoli. Oxygen is transferred from air into the blood in the alveoli.

There are 2 staging systems for small cell lung
cancer (SCLC).
 VA (Veterans Administration) system
 TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) system
What is the VA staging
system?
The VA Lung Study Group created the first
staging system for SCLC. It has been used in
studies on treatment. The system divides lung
cancer into 2 stages:
 Limited stage
 Extensive stage
Limited-stage cancer is found on one side of
the chest and can be treated with radiation
therapy. The cancer is contained in an are

[소세포폐암 환자 가이드라인 | p.14 | lung cancer patient treatment guideline]
ge cancer is found on one side of
the chest and can be treated with radiation
therapy. The cancer is contained in an area
that would fit within one radiation field.
With modern radiation treatment techniques,
the definition of limited-stage disease has been
expanded to include some cases that are on
both sides of the chest as long as they can be
safely treated with radiation.
Most people with SCLC have extensive stage.
Extensive-stage cancer can’t be treated within
one radiation field with the intent to cure the
cancer. It has spread too much.
For example, it may have spread to the other
side of the chest, to the fluid around the lungs
or heart, or outside the chest.

What is the TNM staging
system?
The TNM stages of SCLC range from stage
0 to stage 4. The more serious the cancer
growth and spread, the higher the stage.
Stage 0 cancers are only in the airways and
are very rare.
Stage 1
Stage 1 cancers consist of one small lung
tumor and have not spread to other body parts.
Stage 1A tumors are 3 centimeters (cm, a little
over 1 inch, or the size of a grape) or smaller.
Stage 1B tumors are larger but don’t exceed 4
cm (roughly an inch and a half, or the size of a
walnut).
Stage 2
Stage 2A cancers are like stage 1 cancers
except larger (up to 5 cm, just about 2 in

walnut).
Stage 2
Stage 2A cancers are like stage 1 cancers
except larger (up to 5 cm, just about 2 inches,
the size of a lime). Stage 2B cancers are
larger (up to 7 cm, about 2.75 inches, the size
of a peach), have started to invade other body
parts, or have multiple tumors in one lobe.
Other 2B cancers consist of one lung tumor
that is no larger than 5 cm and has spread to
lymph nodes inside the lung.
Stage 3
Stage 3 is a mixed group of locally advanced
cancers. They are further grouped as stages

The classic treatment for small cell lung cancer

Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays

certain symptoms caused by extensive-stage

Treatment response
A treatment response is how well someone
improves with treatment and how much the
cancer shrinks. Many SCLCs respond strongly
to initial treatment. The timing of assessing the
treatment response differs between treatment
types and the cancer stage.
For limited-stage cancer, the treatment
response should be assessed:
 After concurrent chemoradiation
 During sequential chemoradiation and
after treatment
 During systemic therapy (without radiation
therapy) and after treatment
For extensive-stage cancer, the treatment
response should be assessed:

For extensive-stage cancer, the treatment
response should be assessed:
 After every 2 to 3 cycles of systemic
therapy and after treatment
To assess the treatment response, you will
repeat some blood and imaging tests.
Your health care providers will assess the
treatment response based on test results.
There are 4 possible treatment responses:

result. There are no signs of cancer.
 Partial remission means that the tumors
have shrunk, and blood results are
returning to normal.
 Stable disease is less than a partial
remission. The cancer is not getting
worse.
 Progressive disease is the cancer getting
worse. Treatment options

receive radiation therapy. Prophylactic cranial
irradiation (PCI) is an option for limited- and
extensive-stage cancer.

4 Initial treatment » Clinical trials
Clinical trials
Therapy may also be available as part of a
clinical trial. A clinical trial is a type of medical
research study and a vital way to assess new
treatment methods.
After being developed and tested in a
laboratory, potential new ways of fighting
cancer need to be studied in people. If found
to be safe and effective in a clinical trial, a
drug, device, or treatment approach may be
approved by the FDA.
Everyone with cancer should carefully consider
all of the treatment options available for their
cancer type, including standard treatments and
clinical trials. Talk to your health care

cancer type, including standard treatments and
clinical trials. Talk to your health care provider
about whether a clinical trial may make sense
for you.
Phases
Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment.
Treatment trials are done in phases.
 Phase 1 trials study the dose, safety,
and side effects of an investigational drug
or treatment approach. They also look for
early signs that the drug or approach is
helpful.
 Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or
approach works against a specific type of
cancer.
 Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach
against a standard treatment. If the
results are good, it may be approved by
the FDA.

 Phase 4 trials study the long-term
safety and benefit of an FDA-approved
treatment.
Who can enroll?
Every clinical trial has rules for joining, called
eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age,
cancer type and stage, treatment history, or
general health. These requirements ensure
that participants are alike in specific ways
in order to compare how they respond to a
specific treatment.

Take time to discuss with family, friends, or

There are many myths and misconceptions

Will I get a placebo?
Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines)
are almost never used alone in cancer clinical
trials. It’s common to receive either a placebo
with a standard treatment or a new drug with
a standard treatment. You’ll be informed if a
placebo is part of a clinical trial before you
enroll.

Do I have to pay to be in a clinical trial?

study sponsor pays for research-related costs,
including the study drug. You may, however,
have costs indirectly related to the trial, such

continue to receive standard cancer care.

insurance. You’re responsible for copays and

Supportive care
Supportive care aims to improve your quality of
life. It’s also sometimes called palliative care,
but it is more than that. Supportive care is
important for everyone and is encouraged for
people at all stages of cancer, not just people
at the end of life.
Supportive care can address many needs. It
includes care for health problems caused by
cancer or cancer treatment. You can get help
with making treatment decisions. You can get
help with the coordination of care between
health providers.
Your supportive care specialist will work with
your oncologists to provide you with the be

health providers.
Your supportive care specialist will work with
your oncologists to provide you with the best
care. Other specialists that may be involved in
your care include:
 Respiratory therapists
 Rehabilitation specialists
 Registered dieticians
 Social workers
Side effects
All cancer treatments can cause unwanted
health issues. Such health issues are called
side effects. Some side effects may be harmful
to your health. Others may just be unpleasant.
Side effects depend on many factors. These
factors include the treatment type, length
or dose of treatment, and the person. Many
effects of treatment resolve after treatment
ends, such as:
 Nausea and vomiting from chemot

effects of treatment resolve after treatment
ends, such as:
 Nausea and vomiting from chemotherapy
 Side effects such as a fever, rash, or
inflammation in vital organs (such as
inflammation in the lungs, liver, or thyroid)
from an immune checkpoint inhibitor
 Fatigue and skin changes from radiation
therapy
 Pain and swelling from surgery
Long-term effects start during treatment and
persist after treatment is done. Less often,
effects start long after treatment has ended.
Ask your treatment team for a complete list of
side effects of your treatments.
Also, tell your treatment team about any new
or worse symptoms you get. There may be
ways to help you feel better

Also, tell your treatment team about any new
or worse symptoms you get. There may be

ways to prevent some side effects. An example
